display.purpose: The machine name, the pairing headline, a screen title. 38 / 36 / 30 / 26pt, weight 600, tracking -0.035em.

title.purpose: A sheet's own heading: Settings, Claude, the screenshot.

action.purpose: The title line of a primary action, over its mono-caps preflight.

row-title.purpose: The name of a thing in a grouped row — a display, a paired device, a setting.

label.purpose: All-caps mono. Every readout heading, status line, unit, path, key and command.

label-wide.purpose: The same label at 2.4pt tracking, for a section heading over a group.

readout.purpose: A measured value, with its unit at 10pt in Text Tertiary.

readout-lead.purpose: The one reading on a card that is the reason to look at it — RTT on Home. Larger than the two beside it, because three numbers at one size is a table.

code.purpose: A verbatim command, a diff line, a tool call's target.

motion.name: state-change
motion.purpose: Every state transition: selection, latch, expand, dim. The default, and the only duration in the system.

motion.name: rise
motion.value: translateY(14px) + opacity — opacity alone under Reduce Motion
motion.purpose: Sheets and drawers: Settings, Claude, the command drawer, the revoke confirm, the keyboard bar, the banner.

motion.name: pulse
motion.purpose: The condition dot. Rate carries meaning: a thin link blinks faster than a healthy one. Suppressed entirely while video is live, and never applied to a lost condition — the square is already saying it.

motion.name: spin
motion.purpose: The activity spinner, and the one loop that keeps running under Reduce Motion. A frozen spinner would say the host stopped answering, which nothing measured.

motion.name: blink
motion.purpose: The caret in a code box and in the typing banner. Step-end, so it is on or off and never mid-fade.

breakpoints.name: measure
breakpoints.purpose: Maximum column width for every screen but the remote view; centred beyond it. Never binds on a phone.

breakpoints.name: wide
breakpoints.purpose: Past this the column becomes two: Home is a picture plus a 320px rail of readings, and the remote view's letterbox rail becomes a 276px dock. A container query on the screen itself, so a tablet in Split View gets the layout its actual width earns.

breakpoints.name: rail
breakpoints.purpose: The readings column in the wide Home layout.

breakpoints.name: dock
breakpoints.purpose: The control column in the wide remote layout.

components.name: Primary Action
components.description: The one way forward on a screen, carrying its own preflight: what the tap does and what it costs.

components.name: Filled Action
components.description: A filled action with no sub-label: Allow once, Copy image, a destructive confirm.

components.name: Outlined Action
components.description: The second choice beside a filled one, at the 44 pt minimum target. Its one-point edge is drawn inside the box so a row of these lines up with a filled sibling of the same declared height, and it is inked in `edge` rather than `stroke`: on a control with no fill the edge is the control, so it is held to the 3:1 non-text threshold a hairline is not.

components.name: Condition Card
components.description: One card, one strip of readings. RTT is set larger than the two beside it, because three numbers at the same size is a table and the eye has to read all of it.

components.name: Grouped Rows
components.description: A run of rows two pixels apart that reads as one object. The outer corners of the run round; the seams between rows do not, so each row is still its own target.

narrative.overview:
VibeWire is a gauge cluster for one machine. Every mark on the glass reports something that was actually measured — round-trip time, packet loss, megabits, the age of the last good frame, how long a tool has been waiting on an answer. Nothing on screen is decoration wearing the costume of information. When a value has not been measured, the panel prints an em dash and holds the space, because an unmeasured value and a measured zero are different facts and the interface is not allowed to blur them.

Nightshift is the second turn of that system. It replaces **Longarm**, which drew the instrument out of hairlines on a near-black ground: every panel was a one-point border, every grouped list a stack of rules, and the accent was cyan. What it kept is the thesis. What changed is what carries the structure:

- **Filled surfaces, not hairlines.** A card is a lighter ground with a large corner, not a box drawn around nothing. Two greys apart survive a phone at minimum brightness outdoors, which a one-point line did not.
- **Violet is the user's colour.** Held keys, focus, Claude, the current selection. Cyan sat close enough to jade on a dim screen that a glance could confuse "the link is healthy" with "I left Command switched on"; violet cannot.
- **Grouped rows are one shape.** A list is a run of rows two points apart whose outer corners round and whose seams do not, so the group reads as one object and each row is still its own target.

And four screens were re-laid-out rather than repainted. **Home shows the Mac instead of describing it** — the last frame is the hero and the way in, so the numbers shrink to one strip. **The thumb-arc hub is gone**; its actions live in a labelled rail in the letterbox band and a drawer that never covers the picture. **Claude's tool calls became a timeline** and its permission prompt moved inline, so answering one no longer hides the sentence explaining it. **Pairing is one hero and one target card** instead of a graphic, two fields, a button and a status line.

The room is dark and stays dark. There is no light mode, no `colorScheme` branching, and no shadow anywhere in the app. Type does the second half of the work: monospace with wide tracking for anything counted or named by the machine, sans for prose the user reads at their own pace. The two never trade jobs.
keyCharacteristics: Dark-only, six tonal grounds, zero shadows
Monospace for measured, sans for prose — never interchangeable
Four signal colours: three for the machine, one reserved for the user
Filled cards and grouped rows instead of borders
Every primary action states its own cost before it is tapped
Motion is 120–180 ms state change; nothing decorative moves beside live video

rules.name: The Split-Voice Rule
rules.body: Jade, sodium and clay report what the Mac is doing. Violet reports what the user is doing. No colour crosses that line, which is what lets a glance in a dark room tell a degrading link from a latched modifier.

rules.name: The Redundant-Channel Rule
rules.body: A lost condition is drawn as a square, every other condition as a circle. Colour alone cannot carry "this is the bad one" for a reader who cannot separate red from green, and the shape costs nothing.

rules.name: The Two-Families Rule
rules.body: Monospace for anything the machine measured or named. Sans for anything a person wrote. They never trade jobs, so the eye learns in one screen which parts of the panel are readings and which are sentences.

rules.name: The Lead-Reading Rule
rules.body: Where three numbers sit in a strip, one of them is why the card exists — RTT, on Home. It is set larger than the other two, because three numbers at the same size is a table and the eye has to read all of it.

rules.name: The Dashed-Is-Provisional Rule
rules.body: Dashed means unmeasured, pending, or unselected. It resolves to a solid stroke the moment the thing becomes real. Dashes are never used decoratively.

rules.name: The Containment-Radius Rule
rules.body: Card 20 → control 16 → inner 12. A control never takes a corner equal to or larger than the thing containing it.

rules.name: The Preflight Rule
rules.body: A primary action always states, in its own sub-label, what it is about to do and what it will cost in time, resolution or bytes.

rules.name: The Hit Shape Rule
rules.body: Any target whose ink does not fill its frame — glyphs, outlines, dashed boxes, caption text — must declare a full-box hit shape. This has caused four separate untappable controls in this codebase.

rules.name: The Consequence Rule
rules.body: A destructive confirmation lists three plain sentences: what is destroyed, what it takes to undo it, and what is *not* affected. The last line is what makes the tap safe to judge one-handed.

rules.name: The Never-Cover-The-Picture Rule
rules.body: Nothing that can be answered, dismissed or ignored is allowed to sit over the Mac's screen. The drawer stops short of the band, the stall card sits above the rail, and the permission prompt is in the transcript. This is the rule the thumb arc broke.

rules.name: The Reduce Motion Rule
rules.body: Reduce Motion is about the vestibular system, not about stillness. What goes is travel, scale and spring — sheets fade in place instead of rising. What stays is anything that would otherwise state something false: the spinner keeps turning, because a frozen one says the Mac stopped answering and nothing measured that.

dos: Do derive every displayed condition from a measured value, through `conditionFrom(...)` / `Condition.from(...)`, so the label and the numbers cannot disagree.
Do print `—` in Text Tertiary for any value the host has not reported, at the size the real value will occupy.
Do reserve Held Violet for state the user created — held modifiers, active selection, focused field, Claude — and jade / sodium / clay for what the Mac is doing.
Do set every measured value, unit, path, key and command in mono, and every sentence in sans.
Do give each primary action a mono-caps sub-label stating its cost.
Do name the failure with its address and verdict — list both transports, their results, and the time of last contact rather than one word for "offline".
Do let a group's corners come from position in the run, never from a prop passed at the call site.
Do state the OKLCH definition in the web token file and derive the Swift literal from it, so the three clients cannot drift.
donts: Don't add a shadow, a gradient, or a light mode.
Don't draw a border around something that already has a fill. Two greys apart is the separation.
Don't spend violet on anything the machine did, or jade on anything the user switched on.
Don't put a control over the Mac's picture that could have gone in the band beside it.
Don't show a spinner where four named steps with real values would say the same thing and survive a failure.
Don't let a value render below 9 pt, whatever the reader's text size.
Don't use a dashed stroke decoratively — it means provisional, everywhere, or it means nothing.
